# A01-S116: Synthetic news

Correspondence extract. Omissions are marked […].

[…]

Good morning
You can read this introduction as usual, or click on the video 
a little further down and listen and watch it in the company of Anna, my synthetic 
assistant.
Anna is created with the program Synthesia [1], which I have been 
playing with for some years now. There is basically nothing new about that.
The new thing is that Bornholm.nu has also jumped into it and now 
presents a synthetic TV news program [2] with news from Bornholm spoken by 
the avatar Bridget. Thus, a significant step has been taken into a new 
world that Danish media have so far stayed out of.
The quality of the Bornholm presenter and my own videos with Anna 
is still, what I would call beta. But development is progressing rapidly 
and especially in the major world languages the level is much higher.
Prior to the Bornholm project, among others, the BBC has experimented 
with avatars for local weather forecasts [3] and Reuters has made entire 
sports news segments like the ones Bornholm.nu produces.
The really interesting and decisive thing is that the technology is now so 
cheap that players like me and Bornholm.nu can play with it. For example, 
this video cost eight dollars to produce.
Such low prices open up many exciting opportunities in both the media and 
communication worlds.
Imagine, for example, a larger company that creates an avatar of 
their director - it can be done in about 15 minutes - and then lets 
the avatar send personalized news and messages to each individual 
employee. They can even be in up to 50 different languages, 
if the company is multinational.
You could also merge all articles from Ritzau's housing robot with an 
avatar modeled after Tina Müller, who hosts Hammerslag. 
We could place synthetic Müllers in front of images of the homes taken 
from Google Streetview and in this way get a video that would be fun and 
fascinating for the involved sellers and buyers.
Likewise, for the municipal elections in about a month, we could throw 
robot-written portraits of every newly elected city council member into the belly 
of Synthesia and let a chosen avatar voice them - for 
example, it could be a prominent political reporter.
Right now, synthetic journalism is entering a development phase where 
we will more often encounter new application ideas. There will undoubtedly arise 
many bad or silly ideas, but among them we will 
probably also see the seeds of more sustainable formats.
The keywords are mass production, multilingualism, and the possibility to 
manipulate creatively.
The last opens up the scary risk of bad guys misusing 
the technology for fake news. But it can also create impressive digital 
stories like In Event of Moon Disaster [4], which with Danish Magnus 
Bjerg last week won an Emmy for letting Nixon voice the speech he 
would have given if the moon landing in 1969 had gone wrong.
And with that, on to the rest of the newsletter.
